sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces the subgrade as the foundation for the entire pavement system, whose uniformity and stability govern both long-term pavement performance and the construction process itself. Lists the subgrade issues a geotechnical engineer should be prepared to address and reminds the reader of environmental/permit obligations during subgrade work.
sections.body: The subgrade provides the foundation for the entire pavement system. Uniformity and stability of the subgrade affect the long-term performance of the pavement and the construction process. Subgrade stability is needed to provide adequate support of the pavement section and to provide an acceptable construction platform. Pavement design begins with identification of the pavement foundation, and construction begins with foundation preparation. Important elements of subgrade preparation include evaluating subgrade stability, subgrade modification to improve stability, and evaluating surface tolerances. A geotechnical engineer experienced in subgrade preparation can address issues with variability of soil conditions, soil with low bearing strength (unconfined compressive strength of about 96 kPa [1 tsf] or less), organic soil, swelling/expansive soil, and frost-susceptible soil. During construction, all measures within the limits of construction must be implemented to control water pollution, soil erosion, and siltation as shown on the plans or required by applicable permit, and all pertinent local, state, and federal laws must be followed.
key_points: The subgrade is the foundation for the whole pavement system; its uniformity and stability govern long-term performance and constructability.
Key subgrade preparation tasks: evaluate stability, modify subgrade to improve stability, and evaluate surface tolerances.
A geotechnical engineer should be prepared to address soil variability, low bearing strength (roughly UCS <= 96 kPa / 1 tsf), organic soil, swelling/expansive soil, and frost-susceptible soil.
Water pollution, erosion, and siltation controls must be implemented per plans/permits, and local, state, and federal laws must be followed.
sections.applicability: Applies at the outset of any concrete pavement project, framing the scope and goals of subgrade preparation.

sections.title: Grading and Compacting Subgrade
sections.summary: Container heading for the grading and compaction requirements of subgrade preparation; its content is developed entirely in the child subsections covering grading operations (4-2.1) and compaction (4-2.2).
key_points: Parent heading covering both grading (4-2.1) and compaction (4-2.2) of the subgrade; no independent content of its own.
sections.applicability: Applies as the organizing heading for all subgrade grading and compaction guidance in this chapter.

sections.title: Grading
sections.summary: Container heading for subgrade grading activities; content is carried entirely by the four child subsections covering pre-grading activities, removal of unsuitable subgrade, protection of grade, and grading operations.
key_points: Parent heading covering pre-grading activities, removal of unsuitable subgrade, protection of grade, and grading operations.
sections.applicability: Applies as the organizing heading for subgrade grading guidance (sections 4-2.1.1 through 4-2.1.4).

sections.title: Pre-Grading Activities
sections.summary: Describes mass grading (cutting high points and filling low areas to design elevation) as the first phase of subgrade preparation, followed by construction staking, and notes the value of independently verifying automated GPS-based grading and staking against conventional survey.
sections.body: Mass grading is the first phase of subgrade preparation. It removes high points and fills low areas to achieve the desired finish elevation, with cut/fill quantities typically addressed during the design phase of the project. Construction staking is the second phase of pre-grading, and it is good practice for the owner/engineer to independently verify staking accuracy. Automated grading equipment using global positioning is commonly used to establish grade; when these systems are employed, it is good practice to periodically verify the results through conventional surveying. Important items to consider during pre-grading include: fill material is usually obtained from cut operations, and the geotechnical report should be used to evaluate its potential for engineered fill; if in-place material is insufficient in quantity or has unacceptable properties, alternate borrow areas must be identified; and it is incumbent upon the contractor to become informed about local subgrade conditions relevant to pre-grading and other construction activities.
key_points: Mass grading (removing high points, filling low areas) is the first phase of subgrade preparation; cut/fill is typically set in design.
Construction staking is the second pre-grading phase; independent verification of staking accuracy is good practice.
GPS-based automated grading equipment results should be periodically checked against conventional surveying.
Cut material intended for engineered fill should be evaluated using the geotechnical report.
If in-place material quantity or quality is inadequate, alternate borrow areas must be identified.
The contractor is responsible for informing itself of local subgrade conditions relevant to construction.
sections.applicability: Applies during the mass grading and staking phases before subgrade compaction begins.

sections.title: Removal of Unsuitable Subgrade
sections.summary: Identifies peat, organic silt, silt, and soils with high organic content as unsuitable subgrade materials, and lists three corrective approaches: replace with similar surrounding subgrade soil, replace with granular material, or alter the soil's properties through compaction or stabilization.
sections.body: When preparing the grade, unsuitable soil can be encountered. Materials such as peat, organic silt, silt, and soil with high organic content are classified as unsuitable. To deal with these materials, consider the following actions: remove and replace with soil similar to the surrounding subgrade; remove and replace with granular material; or alter the properties of the material through compaction or stabilization.
key_points: Unsuitable subgrade materials include peat, organic silt, silt, and soils with high organic content.
Corrective option 1: remove and replace with soil similar to the surrounding subgrade.
Corrective option 2: remove and replace with granular material.
Corrective option 3: alter the material's properties through compaction or stabilization.
sections.applicability: Applies when peat, organic silt, silt, or other high-organic-content soils are encountered while grading the subgrade.

sections.title: Protection of Grade
sections.summary: During grading operations, protect the exposed grade through two essential activities: providing temporary drainage to prevent ponding and softening of the subgrade, and managing site traffic so it is distributed over the grade rather than channelized in one area.
sections.body: During grading operations, protect the grade by performing two essential activities. First, provide temporary drainage: trenches, drains, or ditches necessary to divert or intercept surface water. If water ponds on the subgrade, the material softens and is damaged by construction traffic, resulting in delays and the need for repairs. Second, implement procedures to manage site traffic over the grade. Channelized traffic patterns over one portion of the grade must not be used; traffic should instead be distributed over the grade.
key_points: Provide temporary drainage (trenches, drains, ditches) to divert/intercept surface water and prevent ponding on the subgrade.
Ponded water softens the subgrade and leads to construction traffic damage, delays, and repairs.
Manage site traffic to distribute it over the grade; do not allow channelized traffic patterns over one portion of the grade.
sections.applicability: Applies throughout active grading operations, before the subgrade is protected by an overlying layer.

sections.title: Grading Operations
sections.summary: Covers embankment construction practices for concrete pavement subgrades: placing material in successive horizontal layers, respecting specified maximum loose lift depths, distributing hauling equipment evenly, beginning placement at the deepest portion of the fill, and mixing subgrade materials across transition zones to reduce differential settlement or frost heave.
sections.body: Grading operations for a concrete pavement may require an embankment. The embankment is constructed by placing material in successive horizontal layers for the full width of the cross-section. Most specifications include a maximum loose depth of fill placement; using thicker fill layers requires the contractor to demonstrate to the engineer that the thicker layer can be compacted to the specified density. During embankment construction, hauling equipment must travel evenly over the entire width of the embankment -- channelized equipment travel can cause permanent deformation and shear failure. Layer placement should begin at the deepest portion of the fill, with subsequent layers constructed approximately parallel to the finished pavement grade line. Where subgrade transitions occur, the subgrade materials should be mixed by disc at the boundary of the transition zone, over a distance of about 30 m (100 ft) along the transition (15 m [50 ft] on either side). This practice reduces the potential for differential settlement or frost heave.
key_points: Embankments are built in successive horizontal layers across the full cross-section width.
Specifications typically cap the loose lift depth; thicker lifts require the contractor to demonstrate adequate compaction to the engineer.
Hauling equipment must travel evenly over the full embankment width to avoid permanent deformation or shear failure from channelized travel.
Begin layer placement at the deepest portion of the fill; build subsequent layers roughly parallel to the finished grade line.
At subgrade transitions, disc-mix materials over about 30 m (100 ft) along the transition zone (15 m [50 ft] each side) to limit differential settlement or frost heave.
sections.applicability: Applies when embankment fill is required to bring a concrete pavement subgrade to finished grade.

sections.title: Compaction
sections.summary: Container heading for subgrade compaction guidance; content is carried entirely by the four child subsections covering compaction requirements, moisture control, moisture-compaction relationships, and nuclear density gauge use.
key_points: Parent heading covering compaction requirements, moisture control, moisture-density relationships, and nuclear density gauge use.
sections.applicability: Applies as the organizing heading for subgrade compaction guidance (sections 4-2.2.1 through 4-2.2.4).

sections.title: Compaction Requirements
sections.summary: Sets the general 95 percent modified Proctor compaction target for subgrade materials with full-time field density control, and gives differentiated minimum densities and depths of compaction for cohesive and cohesionless soils in both fill and cut sections, plus the traffic-weight threshold for choosing modified versus standard Proctor.
sections.body: Subgrade compaction is essential to building a stable work platform. Due to the weight of construction equipment, good practice is to compact all subgrade materials to 95 percent of the maximum density using the modified Proctor test (ASTM D1557/CRD-C 162), which helps provide a stable working platform. Field density control is a full-time function, allowing observation of the material as it is placed; if the material appears to change, one-point field Proctor tests are used to check the maximum density. Typical requirements are: use the modified Proctor test (ASTM D1557/CRD-C 162) to determine maximum density for pavements trafficked by aircraft/vehicles greater than 27,215 kg (60,000 lb), and use the standard Proctor test (ASTM D698/CRD-C 653) for lighter aircraft/vehicles. For cohesive soil (plasticity index greater than 5 or liquid limit greater than 25) used in fill sections, compact the entire fill to 90 percent maximum density. For cohesive soils in cut sections, compact the top 150 mm (6 in.) to 90 percent maximum density. For cohesionless soil (PI equal to or less than 5 and LL equal to or less than 25) used in fill sections, compact the top 150 mm (6 in.) of fill to 100 percent maximum density, with layers below compacted to 95 percent maximum density. For cohesionless soil in cut sections, compact the top 150 mm (6 in.) to 100 percent maximum density and the next 450 mm (18 in.) to 95 percent maximum density. If the natural subgrade already exhibits densities equal to or greater than the specified densities, no compaction is required other than that needed for a smooth surface, usually just surface rolling.
key_points: General target: compact subgrade to 95% of maximum density per the modified Proctor test (ASTM D1557/CRD-C 162); field density control is full-time.
Use modified Proctor for aircraft/vehicles > 27,215 kg (60,000 lb); use standard Proctor (ASTM D698/CRD-C 653) for lighter traffic.
Cohesive soil (PI > 5 or LL > 25) in fill: compact the entire fill to 90% maximum density.
Cohesive soil in cut sections: compact the top 150 mm (6 in.) to 90% maximum density.
Cohesionless soil (PI <= 5, LL <= 25) in fill: top 150 mm (6 in.) to 100%, layers below to 95% maximum density.
Cohesionless soil in cut sections: top 150 mm (6 in.) to 100%, next 450 mm (18 in.) to 95% maximum density.
If natural subgrade already meets or exceeds specified densities, only surface rolling for smoothness is required.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever subgrade fill or cut material is being compacted to receive a concrete pavement section.

sections.title: Moisture Control
sections.summary: Specifies target moisture windows during subgrade compaction: within +/-2 percent of optimum in general, 1 to 3 percent above optimum for expansive soils to reduce swell potential, and 1 to 2 percent below optimum for non-swelling fine-grained soils; also flags that wet-of-optimum cohesive soils can be unstable under traffic even at target density.
sections.body: Moisture control is essential to obtain a stable subgrade. Compaction specifications usually require the moisture content in the subgrade to be within +/- 2 percent of optimum moisture content before rolling to obtain the prescribed compaction. For expansive soils, moisture content must be 1 to 3 percent above optimum before compaction to reduce swell potential. For fine-grained soils that do not exhibit swelling properties, keep the moisture content 1 to 2 percent below optimum. Cohesive soils compacted wet of optimum can become unstable under construction traffic even when the target density is achieved.
key_points: General moisture window: within +/-2% of optimum moisture content before rolling.
Expansive soils: moisture 1 to 3% above optimum before compaction, to reduce swell potential.
Non-swelling fine-grained soils: keep moisture 1 to 2% below optimum.
Cohesive soils compacted wet of optimum can be unstable under construction traffic even at the target density.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever subgrade moisture must be conditioned prior to compaction rolling.

sections.title: Moisture Compaction Relationships
sections.summary: Explains that moisture-density (Proctor) curves reveal soil compaction sensitivity -- illustrated by Figure 4-1 for a moisture-sensitive clayey sand -- and gives roller-selection and moisture-control practices for cohesive versus cohesionless subgrade soils.
sections.body: Moisture density curves of typical soils can provide insight into field performance. In Figure 4-1, the shape of the curve suggests that clayey sand soil is moisture sensitive: a small change in moisture content results in compaction difficulty. Additional compaction-related items to consider include: use sheepsfoot rollers for cohesive soil, with pads that must penetrate 70 percent of the lift thickness; disc cohesive soil as necessary to control moisture; use static steel drum rollers to smooth the surface of the grade after compaction; and use vibratory steel drum rollers for cohesionless soil, applying vibration with caution if the water table is close to the surface or if subgrade soils are saturated.
key_points: Moisture-density (Proctor) curve shape indicates a soil's moisture sensitivity; clayey sand is an example of a moisture-sensitive soil.
Figure 4-1 illustrates typical moisture-density curves used to assess this sensitivity.
Use sheepsfoot rollers for cohesive soil; pads must penetrate 70% of the lift thickness.
Disc cohesive soil as needed to control moisture content.
Use static steel drum rollers to smooth the grade surface after compaction.
Use vibratory steel drum rollers for cohesionless soil, but apply vibration with caution near a shallow water table or in saturated subgrade.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting compaction equipment and technique based on soil type and moisture sensitivity.

sections.title: Nuclear Density Gauge
sections.summary: Covers nuclear density gauge use for checking compacted subgrade density, including the need for calibration to local materials, and troubleshooting techniques when target densities are difficult to achieve, such as additional moisture-density testing, sand cone verification, and probing for soft layers.
sections.body: Nuclear density testing can check the density of the compacted soil; gauges should be calibrated to local materials. If problems achieving density are encountered, use the following troubleshooting techniques: perform additional moisture-density testing to ensure the proper maximum density value is used to control field compaction; use a sand cone or volume measure to perform density tests; use traditional methods to determine moisture content; and probe the subgrade to determine if soft layers are present below the problem area.
key_points: Nuclear density gauges must be calibrated to local materials before use.
If density problems occur, perform additional moisture-density testing to confirm the maximum density value used for control.
Cross-check with a sand cone or volume measure test method.
Cross-check moisture content using traditional (non-nuclear) methods.
Probe the subgrade to check for soft layers beneath the problem area.
sections.applicability: Applies during field density testing of compacted subgrade and when troubleshooting compaction-density problems.

sections.title: Subgrade Stabilization
sections.summary: Explains why subgrades are stabilized (low strength, swelling potential, construction schedule), points to UFC 3-250-11 for detailed stabilization methods, flags fine-grained soils with unconfined compressive strength <= 190 kPa (2 tsf) as a stability concern, and lists three localized-area remediation procedures.
sections.body: Subgrades are often stabilized for one of the following reasons: to improve low strength soil, to reduce swelling potential, or to improve construction conditions. Unsuitable subgrade conditions can delay construction due to the time required to implement appropriate measures, and a stabilized subgrade helps maintain schedule -- important on projects requiring timely pavement opening to traffic. Details on stabilization are found in UFC 3-250-11, Soil Stabilization and Modification for Pavements. If the site contains fine-grained soils, a contingency plan for stabilization should be prepared in case unsuitable soils are encountered in localized pockets; fine-grained soils with unconfined compressive strengths of 190 kPa (2 tsf) or less usually present stability problems. For localized areas, consider the following procedures: remove soft or disturbed material and replace with subgrade material from adjacent areas (works for surficial disturbance); remove soft or disturbed material and replace with crushed stone, using geotextile fabric to prevent subgrade intrusion into the stone layer if the disturbed layer's unconfined compressive strength is 96 kPa (1 tsf) or less; or place a geogrid over the soft area and place and compact 250 mm (10 in.) of crushed stone on top of the geogrid to distribute the load to the subgrade.
key_points: Subgrades are stabilized to improve low-strength soil, reduce swelling potential, or improve construction conditions/schedule.
UFC 3-250-11, Soil Stabilization and Modification for Pavements, provides stabilization details.
Fine-grained soils with unconfined compressive strength <= 190 kPa (2 tsf) usually present stability problems; prepare a contingency stabilization plan.
Localized fix 1: remove soft/disturbed material and replace with adjacent subgrade material (surficial disturbance only).
Localized fix 2: remove soft/disturbed material and replace with crushed stone; use geotextile fabric if the layer's UCS <= 96 kPa (1 tsf).
Localized fix 3: place a geogrid over the soft area, then place and compact 250 mm (10 in.) of crushed stone on top to distribute load.
sections.applicability: Applies when subgrade soils exhibit low strength, swelling potential, or otherwise threaten the construction schedule, requiring stabilization.

sections.title: Acceptance of Grade
sections.summary: Covers grade adjustment strategy for unstabilized versus stabilized subgrade materials -- scarify/cut/fill for unstabilized, build high and trim for stabilized -- and gives the numeric acceptance criteria for a finished grade: maximum surface deviation and maximum surface elevation deviation.
sections.body: For unstabilized materials, consider scarifying, cutting, or filling areas to adjust the grade, if needed. With stabilized materials, filling in thin lifts is not possible; therefore, construct the grade high and trim to final grade. For large projects, consider using an autograder or trimmer to minimize grade problems. Use the following criteria to accept a finished grade: surface deviation, a maximum of 10 mm (3/8 in.) based on a 3.6 m (12 ft) straightedge; and surface elevation, a maximum deviation of +/-13 mm (0.5 in.).
key_points: Unstabilized materials: adjust grade by scarifying, cutting, or filling as needed.
Stabilized materials: cannot be filled in thin lifts, so construct the grade high and trim to final grade.
Large projects should consider an autograder or trimmer to minimize grade problems.
Acceptance criterion -- surface deviation: max 10 mm (3/8 in.) over a 3.6 m (12 ft) straightedge.
Acceptance criterion -- surface elevation: max deviation of +/-13 mm (0.5 in.).
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating whether a finished subgrade meets the surface tolerance criteria for acceptance.

sections.title: Protection of Grade
sections.summary: Once the finished subgrade is accepted, a traffic control plan must be implemented because heavy construction trucks can damage the prepared surface; any ruts or rough places that develop must be smoothed and re-compacted before the subbase is placed.
sections.body: Once the grade is accepted, implement a traffic control plan. Heavy construction trucks traveling on the prepared surface can damage the grade; traffic management must be enforced if logistics require use of the prepared grade by construction equipment. All ruts or rough places that develop in a completed subgrade must be smoothed and re-compacted prior to placing the subbase.
key_points: Implement a traffic control plan once the subgrade is accepted, since heavy trucks can damage the finished surface.
Enforce traffic management whenever construction equipment must use the prepared grade.
Smooth and re-compact any ruts or rough places before subbase placement.
sections.applicability: Applies to the period between subgrade acceptance and subbase placement, when the finished grade remains exposed to construction traffic.

sections.title: Adverse Weather Conditions
sections.summary: Container heading for subgrade guidance under adverse weather; content is carried entirely by the child subsections on drainage, freezing temperatures, and the troubleshooting guide.
key_points: Parent heading covering drainage practices, freezing-temperature protection, and a subgrade troubleshooting guide.
sections.applicability: Applies as the organizing heading for adverse-weather subgrade guidance (sections 4-5.1 through 4-5.3).

sections.title: Drainage
sections.summary: Requires drainage provisions and positive slope to be maintained at every stage of subgrade preparation, describes discing/drying when moisture is above optimum, and calls for sealing the subgrade surface with a rubber-tired or steel drum roller ahead of expected rain to avoid serious moisture-related problems.
sections.body: Implement provisions for drainage at each stage during subgrade preparation, maintaining a positive slope to assure drainage. When subgrade moisture content is above optimum, consider discing and drying to reduce the moisture content. If rain is expected after the subgrade is prepared for compaction, seal the subgrade surface using a rubber-tired or steel drum roller; if this is not done in time, serious problems can develop due to excess moisture in the subgrade.
key_points: Maintain drainage provisions and positive slope at every stage of subgrade preparation.
If moisture content is above optimum, disc and dry the subgrade to reduce it.
Seal the subgrade surface with a rubber-tired or steel drum roller ahead of expected rain to prevent serious moisture problems.
sections.applicability: Applies throughout subgrade preparation whenever drainage control or an approaching rain event must be managed.

sections.title: Freezing Temperatures
sections.summary: Requires scarifying and re-compacting the top 150 mm (6 in.) of subgrade exposed to freezing, both when freezing conditions occur during active preparation and when grading work resumes in spring after a winter shutdown.
sections.body: If a subgrade is subject to freezing, scarify the surface of the subgrade to a depth of at least 150 mm (6 in.) and re-compact. If grade preparation was halted for winter, scarify the exposed subgrade surface to a depth of at least 150 mm (6 in.) and recompact prior to continuing grading the following spring.
key_points: Subgrade exposed to freezing: scarify to at least 150 mm (6 in.) depth and re-compact.
After a winter work stoppage: scarify the exposed surface to at least 150 mm (6 in.) and recompact before resuming grading in spring.
sections.applicability: Applies to subgrades exposed to freezing temperatures, whether during active preparation or after a winter construction shutdown.

sections.title: Troubleshooting Guide
sections.summary: Introduces and enumerates Table 4-1, a Problem/Probable Cause/Corrective Action diagnostic table covering three common subgrade field problems: a loose-appearing surface, depressions or excessive roller movement, and a surface that varies from coarse to fine.
sections.body: Table 4-1 lists various subgrade problems, probable causes, and corrective actions encountered during subgrade preparation. If the surface appears loose, the probable cause is low density; the corrective action is to check moisture content and density, then re-condition to optimum moisture and re-compact the area. If depressions or excessive movement occur under the roller, the probable cause is either high moisture content or a weak layer under the surface; the corrective action is to check moisture content and re-condition to optimum if high, probe the grade with a dynamic cone penetrometer (DCP) to find the weak layer, and stabilize the area. If the surface varies from coarse to fine, the probable cause is segregation of imported material or a change of material; the corrective action is to perform a sieve analysis to check gradation and mix and re-compact the surface.
key_points: Problem: surface appears loose. Cause: low density. Action: check moisture content and density; re-condition to optimum moisture and re-compact.

Problem: depressions or excessive movement under roller. Cause: high moisture content or a weak layer under the surface. Action: check/re-condition moisture, probe with DCP to find the weak layer, and stabilize the area.
Problem: surface varies from coarse to fine. Cause: segregation of imported material or a change of material. Action: perform a sieve analysis to check gradation and mix and re-compact the surface.
Table 4-1 is a Problem / Probable Cause / Corrective Action diagnostic table for subgrade field issues.
sections.applicability: Applies when diagnosing and correcting field problems observed on a prepared subgrade during compaction.
